name: Codenames
desc: The word association party game that took the world by storm. Split into two teams, spymasters give one-word clues to guide their teammates to the right words, but watch out for the assassin.
why: Easy to teach, plays up to 8, always different. Best party game for non-gamers.

name: Wavelength
desc: A mind-reading party game where you try to guess where your teammate is pointing on a hidden spectrum. Hot to cold, easy to hard, the tension is real.
why: Perfect for groups that love conversation and debate. Every round is different.

name: Herd Mentality
desc: You get points for thinking like the majority. The twist? If your answer is unique, you get nothing. Don't be the pink cow.
why: Hilarious with big groups. The only game where copying answers is the smart play.

name: Blank Slate
desc: A word association game where you pick a cue card and write a word that completes the phrase. Match with another player to score.
why: Simple enough for kids, fun enough for adults. Great icebreaker.

name: Sushi Go!
desc: A fast-paced card drafting game where you're trying to grab the best combination of sushi dishes before they pass by. Think 7 Wonders, but simpler and cuter.
why: Under $12, plays in 15 minutes, and adorable. Best value in board gaming.

name: Just One (2025 Refresh)
desc: A cooperative word association game where everyone helps one player guess a secret word. The catch? If any two players write the same clue, both clues are discarded. Simple, brilliant, and tense.
why: Won Spiel des Jahres 2019 for a reason. Cooperative so nobody gets singled out. Best with 5-7.

name: Decrypto
desc: A word deduction game where two teams encrypt secret words while trying to intercept the other team's clues. Each clue must stay subtle enough that your partner gets it, but loose enough that the enemy cannot crack your code.
why: The deeper sibling of Codenames. More tension, no instant elimination, and the best pick for groups that want to actually think.

name: Telestrations (6 Player 2nd Edition)
desc: A friendly drawing and guessing game, essentially telephone with doodles. Every player starts with a word, secretly draws it, passes the sketch, guesses what it is, then passes again. By the time the book comes around, the original word is a distant memory and everyone is laughing.
why: The best big-group icebreaker. Nobody gets singled out, every player is busy every round, and terrible drawing skills make it funnier, not worse.

name: King of Tokyo (New Edition)
desc: A Yahtzee-style dice game where giant monsters battle for control of Tokyo. Roll six dice three times, punch the monster in the city, heal outside it, and hoard energy to buy power cards. First to 20 victory points or last monster standing wins.
why: The gateway dice game. Ten minute teach, huge laughs, and it never wears out its welcome at a full table.

name: Camel Up (Second Edition)
desc: A betting and racing party game where camels stack on top of each other and nobody can predict the finish. Roll a die to move a camel, place a bet, or drop a tile, then watch the whole table react. Spiel des Jahres winner.
why: The best game for a mixed group of five or more. Everyone stays involved every round, and the chaos is the point.

name: Catan (6th Edition)
desc: The game that launched modern board gaming. Trade, build, and settle on the island of Catan. Dice rolls determine resources, but your strategy determines who wins.
why: The perfect gateway game. If you want one game to start your collection, this is it.

name: Carcassonne
desc: Draw a tile, place it, claim it with a meeple. The classic tile-laying game where one quiet decision per turn builds a shared medieval world of cities, roads, and fields.
why: The purest gateway game. Ten seconds to learn, a lifetime to master, and it never overstays its welcome.

name: Carcassonne: Hunters and Gatherers
desc: A stand-alone Stone Age take on Carcassonne. Hunters lie in the meadows, gatherers stand in the forests, fishers work the rivers, and huts score off the fish in a river system. Each player gets 5 tribe members and 2 huts, and its 79 tiles do not mix with the base game.
why: The best alternative for a table that has played the original 50 times. Different terrain, same elegant one-tile-per-turn rhythm.

name: Ticket to Ride (2025 Refresh)
desc: Build train routes across America. Connect cities, complete destination tickets, and block your opponents. Simple to learn, impossible to master.
why: The most successful modern board game for a reason. Routes, risk, and rail-building fun. Refreshed in 2025 with new art, bigger cards, and 33 destination tickets.

name: Ticket to Ride: Europe (2026 Refresh)
desc: The European map adds tunnels, ferries, and train stations on top of the classic route-building. Slightly deeper than the base game, just as easy to teach.
why: The upgrade for groups that already know the base game. Tunnels and stations add real decisions without much extra reading.

name: Ticket to Ride: First Journey
desc: A kid-friendly version of Ticket to Ride with a shorter map and simpler tickets. Connect cities across North America without the long reading.
why: The best way to pull a 6-year-old into the hobby. Same core idea as the grown-up game, half the rules.

name: Azul
desc: A stunning tile-laying game inspired by Portuguese azulejo tiles. Draft beautiful ceramic tiles and place them on your board. Gorgeous components, sharp strategy.
why: Looks amazing on the table, plays fast, and the 'take that' moments are brutal.

name: Azul: Summer Pavilion
desc: The third Azul, and the most forgiving one. Same pick and place bones as the original, but the board is looser, the wild tiles let you finish more rows, and a bad round is a scratch instead of a knockout.
why: The best Azul for two players. It keeps the tension and drops the knockout blows, so a bad round is a scratch instead of a lost game.

name: Cascadia
desc: A captivating tile-laying game about building ecosystems. Place habitat tiles and wildlife tokens to create the most harmonious Pacific Northwest environment.
why: The definition of 'easy to learn, hard to master.' Also plays solo.

name: Calico
desc: A quilt and cats tile puzzle from the makers of Cascadia. Draft patch tiles, build color groups to earn buttons, and attract cats by matching patterns on a board that fills to the last space.
why: Tighter and more punishing than Cascadia. Best for players who enjoy a puzzle that punishes one bad placement.

name: Wingspan
desc: An engine-building game where you attract birds to your preserve. Each bird has unique abilities and habitat requirements. Stunning artwork, relaxing vibe.
why: The most beautiful game on this list. Deep enough for veterans, inviting for newcomers.

name: Wyrmspan
desc: The dragon version of Wingspan from Stonemaier Games. Excavate a cave system, walk an adventurer meeple down it to wake the dragons roosting there, and hatch young dragons that grow into stronger ones. 183 dragon cards, deeper combos, longer turns.
why: The next step up for a table that loves Wingspan and wants more crunch. Designed by Connie Vogelmann, developed by Elizabeth Hargrave.

name: 7 Wonders (New Edition)
desc: The legendary card-drafting game. 3 to 7 players build their ancient civilization from a passing hand of cards, each round picking one to keep and sending the rest around the table. Three ages of build, trade, and quiet denial. Won the 2011 Kennerspiel des Jahres.
why: The game that made drafting mainstream. 30 minutes, everyone plays at once, nobody waits. The step up from casual to real strategy.

name: Dominion (Second Edition)
desc: The game that invented deck-building. Every player starts with the same ten cards and buys more from the kingdom row, thinning and upgrading their deck each turn. First to the most victory points when the piles run dry wins. An entire genre grew from this one box.
why: The purest deck-builder ever made. Two minutes to teach, a lifetime to fail at, and it hits perfectly at three players.

name: Everdell (3rd Edition)
desc: A breathtaking worker placement game set in a woodland valley. Through the four seasons of a single year, place your critter workers to gather resources, build a city of creatures and constructions, and prepare for the hard winter before the moon rises.
why: The prettiest heavy-ish game on the shelf. You are done learning it fast, then the combos pull you back every single game. Best at exactly 4.

name: Sagrada
desc: A dice-drafting puzzle where you build a stained glass window out of colored dice. Every space on your board restricts what fits, and public plus secret objectives decide the most beautiful window.
why: The dice take on Azul. Sharp, quiet, and gorgeous on the table. My pick for the nights Azul starts to feel solved.

name: Splendor
desc: Collect gem tokens, buy development cards, and attract nobles to your court. Simple mechanics with satisfying strategic depth.
why: 30 minutes, easy rules, but every game feels different. Family favorite.

name: Kingdomino
desc: Draft domino tiles to build your kingdom. Each tile has two terrain types, match them strategically to score big. Quick, clever, and addictive.
why: Gold standard for family games. Cheap, fast, fun for all ages.

name: Knitting Circle
desc: A standalone follow-up to Calico. Players are knitters laying yarn tiles into patterns, chasing the coziest project on the table. Same cozy spatial puzzle, easier scoring, cheaper box.
why: The gentlest way into the Calico family of tile puzzles, and the cheapest.

name: Sequence
desc: A classic strategy game combining cards and board. Play a card, place a chip. Get five in a row and you win. Simple tension that keeps everyone engaged.
why: Plays up to 12. Grandma-friendly. Proven for 40+ years.

name: Castle Combo
desc: A charming tableau-building game where you construct medieval castles. Draft cards, build combos, and watch your kingdom grow. Quick to learn, satisfying to play.
why: 2026's breakout family hit. Try it on Board Game Arena first.

name: Quacks Board Game
desc: A push-your-luck bag-building game. Draw ingredients from your bag to brew potions. Draw too many white cherries and your potion explodes. Tense, hilarious, and addictive.
why: Every pull is a gamble. The 'push your luck' mechanic keeps everyone engaged.

name: Dixit
desc: A storytelling game of imagination. One player gives a cryptic clue about a dreamlike card, others play cards that match the clue, and everyone guesses which card belongs to the storyteller. Beautiful art, infinite creativity.
why: Spiel des Jahres winner. Works with creative kids and adults alike. Every game is different.

name: Wingspan Pocket
desc: Wingspan shrunk into a small box. You activate a single row of cards per turn, and the bird powers are printed as icons instead of sentences. Stand-alone game, and its cards do not mix with the base box.
why: The version that lives in a bag. Same bird-collecting feeling in 30 minutes, for about $20.

name: Patchwork
desc: A two-player tetris-like game where you piece together a quilt. Buy patches with buttons, place them strategically, and cover your board efficiently.
why: Best 2-player game ever made. Period. Perfect date night game.

name: 7 Wonders Duel
desc: The two-player version of the classic 7 Wonders. Draft cards in a pyramid formation, build structures, and compete for military and scientific supremacy.
why: Better than the original 7 Wonders. Tense, strategic, and deeply satisfying.

name: Fox in the Forest
desc: A trick-taking card game designed specifically for two players. Special powers on every card, and winning too many tricks is just as dangerous as winning too few.
why: Under $15, plays in 20 minutes, and the 'avoid winning' mechanic is brilliant.

name: Jaipur
desc: A fast-paced trading game set in the bustling city of Jaipur. Buy and sell goods, earn bonuses for sets, and outsmart your opponent in the marketplace.
why: The quintessential 2-player card game. Quick rounds, big decisions.

name: Lost Cities
desc: A risk-management card game about exploration. Invest in expeditions, manage your hand, and decide when to cut your losses. Push your luck across five ancient cities.
why: Reiner Knizia's masterpiece. Elegant, tense, and endlessly replayable.

name: Hanamikoji
desc: A beautifully crafted card game set in a geisha house. Win the favor of geishas by playing sets of cards. Four action slots but only four moves per round. Every decision is agonizing.
why: The most elegant 2-player card game ever made. 7 actions per game, infinite depth.

name: Splendor Duel
desc: The two-player rebuild of Splendor, remade from the ground up by Marc Andre and Bruno Cathala. Same gems and engine-building core, tighter board, and three separate ways to win instead of one.
why: Fixes the thing the base game does worst: two-player Splendor has no tension. This one has plenty.

name: Love Letter
desc: A deduction game of risk and luck with only 16 cards. Deliver a love letter to the princess while eliminating rival suitors. Tiny box, huge fun.
why: 16 cards. $13. 20 minutes. The best game-per-dollar ratio in board gaming.

name: The Crew: The Quest for Planet Nine
desc: A cooperative trick-taking game set in space. Each mission has unique objectives, you must communicate without talking and win the right tricks together.
why: The game that redefined trick-taking. Co-op, campaign-based, and incredibly clever.

name: Uno
desc: The classic family card game that needs no introduction. Match colors and numbers, use action cards to mess with opponents, and never forget to yell 'UNO!'
why: Under $12, everyone knows the rules, and it never gets old.

name: Skull King
desc: A trick-taking game with pirates, mermaids, and the terrifying Skull King himself. Bid how many tricks you'll win, then try to hit your target exactly.
why: The best bidding trick-taking game since Spades. Perfect for 4-6 players.

name: Star Realms
desc: A fast-paced deck-building card game. Buy ships and bases, then attack your opponent directly. Combos chain into devastating turns. Plays in 20 minutes.
why: Best deck-building game for the price. Portable, fast, and deep.

name: Coup
desc: A social deduction game of bluffing and bribery. You hold two influence cards with unique powers. Bluff, bribe, and call out other players before they take you down. A 15 minute game of pure tension.
why: The ultimate bluffing game. Pocket-sized, fast, and every round ends in betrayal.

name: Sky Team
desc: A two-player cooperative dice game about landing an airliner. Pilot and co-pilot each roll four dice behind a screen, then place them in silence on a cockpit panel: axis, engines, flaps, gear, radio and brakes. Seven rounds, twenty airports.
why: Spiel des Jahres 2024 and the first strictly two-player winner. Tense, quick, and it teaches you to read a partner instead of talking over them.

name: Pandemic
desc: Work together to stop global outbreaks. Each player has a unique role: medic, scientist, dispatcher. You must cure four diseases before time runs out.
why: The gateway co-op game. Tension, teamwork, and that 'one more game' feeling.

name: Forbidden Island
desc: A cooperative race against time. Collect ancient treasures from a sinking island before it disappears. The island sinks more every turn, tension builds fast.
why: Pandemic's little brother. Cheaper, faster, but just as tense.

name: Horrified
desc: A cooperative monster-fighting game where you team up against classic movie monsters. Dracula, Frankenstein, the Mummy, each has unique mechanics.
why: The best entry-level co-op. Theme is perfect, difficulty scales well.

name: Mysterium
desc: One player is a ghost communicating through surreal dream cards. The others are psychics trying to solve a murder. Beautiful art, unique mechanics, no two games are alike.
why: The cooperative Clue. Gorgeous components, great for creative groups.

name: Castle Panic
desc: Defend your castle against waves of monsters. Play cards to hit, arrow, and bash approaching threats before they destroy your walls. Made for kids and adults to play together.
why: Great with kids. Co-op so no one gets eliminated. Real tension.

name: The Grizzled
desc: A cooperative card game set in World War I. You are soldiers in the trenches. Every round brings new threats and trauma cards. Communication is limited. Survive until the armistice together.
why: The most thematically rich co-op card game. Hard, emotional, and unique.

name: Wingspan (Solo Mode)
desc: Play the full Wingspan experience solo against an automa opponent. The bird engine-building is just as satisfying alone, and the automa is surprisingly smart.
why: Best solo mode in modern gaming. Relaxing, strategic, and beautiful.

name: Sprawlopolis
desc: A tiny wallet game with huge depth. Build a city by placing cards, each with scoring conditions. 18 cards, infinite combinations. The ultimate travel solo game.
why: Fits in your pocket. 20 minute plays. Infinite replayability. $13.

name: Friday
desc: A solitaire deck-building game set on a desert island. You are Friday, helping Robinson survive by fighting hazards with a deck of cards you constantly trim and upgrade. Brutal, clever, and endlessly replayable.
why: The $20 deck builder that taught me how to lose well. Rules in ten minutes, punishing in a good way.

name: Final Girl
desc: A solo horror movie game. Play as the final girl trying to survive a slasher killer. Each scenario feels like a different movie. High tension, big decisions, brutal outcomes.
why: The gold standard for solo gaming. Every game tells a story.

name: Under Falling Skies
desc: A dice placement game where you defend Earth from alien invasion. Each dice pip becomes a ship or research action. Campaign mode adds persistent upgrades and story.
why: Best pure solo game. Dice placement meets tower defense. Campaign is brilliant.

name: Spirit Island
desc: The ultimate solo puzzle. Play as a nature spirit defending your island from colonizers. Unique powers, deep strategy, and every game is a brain-burning challenge.
why: The most respected solo game on BGG (8.5 rating). Not for beginners, but unmatched depth.
